{#sayt} **Results: **The mean age of the total study population was 69 ± 13, and 1530 (40.8%) of them were female. Finally, 188 (5.0%) patients died in the hospital and 766 (20.4%) patients died during a one-year follow-up. Patients in the higher SHR group had a longer hospital stay (2.7% vs. 2.4%, *p* < 0.001) and higher in-hospital mortality (8 vs. 7, *p* < 0.001) than those in the lower group. The Kaplan–Meier curves also show that higher SHR is associated with an elevated risk of one-year mortality in patients with HF, both in the DM and non-DM groups (all log-rank *p* < 0.0001). As a continuous variable, SHR was an independent predictor for one-year mortality [hazard ratio (HR), 2.893; 95% confidence interval (CI), 2.198–3.808]. Elevated SHR was significantly associated with higher risk of one-year mortality in patients with (HR, 1.499; 95% CI, 1.104–2.036) and without DM (HR, 1.300; 95% CI, 1.096–1.542), consistently. The RCS curve shows a gradual increase in the probability of one-year mortality as the value of SHR increases for HF patients.

{#xk1u} # Discussion

{#nytx} In this present study, we examined the predictive value of SHR for the risk of one-year mortality among HF patients from MIMIC-IV database, regardless of the status of DM. Our findings demonstrate that a higher SHR is correlated with a higher risk of one-year mortality in patients with HF, irrespective of the presence of DM. Specifically, the adjusted hazard ratios suggest that an elevated SHR is associated with an 88.1% increased risk of one-year mortality in HF patients with DM and a 27.8% increased risk in those without DM. Additionally, we explore the effect of SHR on one-year mortality according to the AHF and CHF groups. Our results suggest that the predictive role of SHR for one-year all-cause mortality is consistent among both AHF and CHF patients. This consistent association across different subgroups underscores the robustness of SHR as a predictor for poor prognosis in HF. The Kaplan–Meier curves also show that higher SHR is associated with an elevated risk of one-year mortality in patients with HF, both in the DM and non-DM groups. The RCS curve shows a gradual increase in the probability of one-year mortality as the value of SHR increases for HF patients with DM. Similarly, for HF patients without DM, the RCS curve also demonstrates a comparable trend. Both curves suggest a negative correlation between SHR and survival probability in HF patients with and without DM.

ops.markdown: It is widely recognized that stress hyperglycemia is linked to elevated mortality and adverse outcomes in critically ill patients [23, 32]. However, intensive glucose-lowering may paradoxically raise the risk of death, making glycemic management challenging [33]; a large-scale international prospective randomized controlled trial found that intensive blood glucose control increased mortality in ICU patients, possibly due to severe hypoglycemia [33]. A retrospective study of 45,000 critically ill patients suggested that a mean blood glucose of 4.4 to 7.8 mmol/L was linked to lower mortality in patients without DM, whereas those with DM tolerated higher levels, with > 6.1 mmol/L conferring lower mortality than 4.4 to 6.1 mmol/L [34]. Moreover, stress hyperglycemia generally suggests a more critical condition. In our study, the high SHR group was older, more often had ACS and CAD, and had higher white blood cell counts and lower hemoglobin levels, all of which confirm a more severe condition and more comorbidities. Therefore, optimal management of HF patients with stress hyperglycemia requires both reasonable glycemic control and rigorous management of HF and co-existing conditions. SHR levels can also be influenced by sepsis, cerebrovascular and cardiovascular diseases, and other critical illnesses [35]; we therefore adjusted for relevant variables, but SHR should still be interpreted with caution. Nutritional status and other diseases may also affect SHR, warranting careful interpretation in such situations [36]. The current ESC guidelines recommend sodium-glucose transporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors for HF patients, regardless of left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF), once the condition is stable [37]. One study suggests that SGLT2 inhibitors may exert cardioprotective effects by inhibiting autophagy in cardiomyocytes, improving survival in mice with MI and acute hyperglycemia [38]. Patients with HF and stress hyperglycemia may derive greater benefit from SGLT2 inhibitors, but further research is needed to confirm.

{#nytx} In this present study, we examined the predictive value of SHR for the risk of one-year mortality among HF patients from MIMIC-IV database, regardless of the status of DM. Our findings demonstrate that a higher SHR is correlated with a higher risk of one-year mortality in patients with HF, irrespective of the presence of DM.
